name: Fronto-occipital cranial modification

card.summary: Fronto-occipital cranial modification is a historical practice of applying pressure to an infant skull front and back to produce a lengthened, sculpted head shape valued as beautiful or high-status.
card.note: Applied to infants; documented asymmetry and tissue injury; not an adult method.

quick.overview:
Fronto-occipital modification is one of the main types of intentional cranial modification, in which boards or bindings press on the forehead and back of an infant skull so it grows into a shaped form. In the cultures that practised it, a reshaped head was an aesthetic ideal and a marker of group identity or status.

Archaeology shows the tradition is ancient: most skulls at the Neolithic Houtaomuga site in northeast China showed this type. Looksmaxxing communities mention it as a historical curiosity in bone-structure discussions.
quick.how: Historically, pressure was applied with bindings, boards or cradleboards during infancy, when the skull is most pliable, typically in the first three years of life. After infancy, the effects are progressively lost as the body partly compensates. Adult use is not documented and no instructions are given here.
quick.risks: Reported harms include marked cranial and facial asymmetry, and bleeding, infection or necrosis of compressed tissue. A study of Peruvian samples found no significant difference in cranial capacity between modified and unmodified skulls.

lead: Fronto-occipital cranial modification is a form of intentional cranial modification, the reshaping of an infant skull by sustained pressure. E. V. Zhirov (1940) named it as one of three main types, alongside round and sagittal.[1] The practice was done for beauty, group affiliation or status, and so belongs to the long history of appearance modification.[1]

The earliest possible cases date to the 8th millennium BCE at Ganj Dareh in western Iran, and the practice appears across Eurasia, the Americas, Oceania and Africa.[1] At the Neolithic Houtaomuga site in Jilin, China, researchers report the earliest evidence and longest in situ practice, with most skulls showing fronto-occipital modification.[2][1]
In looksmaxxing discussion it is cited as history. Because it works only on the infant skull, it is not an adult technique.

chain: Pressure on forehead and back of infant skull
Skull grows into a lengthened shape
angle.text: In the societies that practised it, the head shape itself was the aesthetic goal. It acts only during infancy, when the skull is pliable.

infobox: Possibly 8th millennium BCE, Ganj Dareh, Iran

paras: Pressure is applied with bindings, boards, cradleboards, cloth or padded devices, usually from birth until the desired shape is reached or the child resists. There is no single accepted classification system.[1]

Hippocrates (c. 400 BCE) described the "Macrocephali", or long-heads. Groups said to practise it include the Yuezhi, Huns and Alans, the Maya, Inca, and Chinookan peoples, and Mangbetu in Africa, and it continued in parts of France into the early twentieth century and still occurs in places such as Vanuatu.[1] Early Neolithic evidence also comes from Houtaomuga, China.[2]

Proposed reasons include signalling ethnicity or status, aesthetic ideals, and association with intelligence or closeness to spirits in some cultures; among the Maya, a reduced occipital bun was linked to courage.[1]
Strong asymmetry and tissue damage such as bleeding, infection or necrosis are reported. A Peruvian study found no significant cranial-capacity difference.[1]
No studies found. Research is archaeological and anthropological, such as the Houtaomuga skull analysis.[2]

timeline.event: First record of the practice among Visayan peoples (Philippines).[1]
Zhirov describes three main types including fronto-occipital.[1]
